newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian rubber prices firm on car industry demand.
newsitem.headline: Indian rubber prices firm on car industry demand.

text.p: Indian rubber prices have firmed on an expected surge in demand from the automobile industry, officials and traders said on Tuesday.
Prices this week were running at 55 rupees per kg compared to 43 rupees at this time last year, and up from 48 rupees in early August, traders said.
Rubber consumers expect increased activity in coming months with the domestic automobile industry heading for rapid growth.
"The auto industry is heading for a 15 percent growth rate," said a spokesman of the All India Rubber Industries Association.
"The new projects of Ford, Mahindra and Hyundai will roll out 100,000 cars annually. This will propel a massive growth in the tyre industry," he said.
"Besides there is an improvement in credit availability, the interest rate is now reasonable. Cash liquidity is seen," said George Thomas, a dealer.
Domestic rubber prices normally soar in June-July as the process of rubber tapping becomes difficult during the monsoon rains in the morning hours, and that affects supplies.

"Our fears that prices would skyrocket in June and July to last year's record of 67 rupees per kg did not materialise because of a steady flow of rubber and low consumption," said Thomas. The prices averaged 50 rupees per kg in July this year.
This year rains fell mainly during the afternoon hours, permitting rubber tapping to continue almost uninterrupted.
The Indian rubber board has estimated output in August at 43,000 tonnes against an estimated consumption of 47,000 tonnes.
"But from September to January 1997, production will exceed consumption each month," said a board member.
The rubber board has projected rubber output in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) at 542,000 tonnes while consumption is estimated at 578,000 tonnes.
The board expects imports of only 10,000 tonnes of rubber in 1996/97, the deficit to be adjusted from carry-forward stocks.
"Till now, no import has taken place. With the commencement of the peak production season, there won't be any need to import in the coming months," dealer Thomas said.
India in its annual budget cut import duty on natural rubber to 20 percent from 25 percent, a move criticised by growers who say it would hit domestic planters.

The chief minister of southern Kerala state, which has more than 90 percent of the country's rubber planters, has said that low prices resulting from import liberalisation would hit the state's 900,000 growers and 325,000 workers.
